name: Dome of the Rock
info: The Dome of the Rock is an octagonal Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, built over the Foundation Stone on the orders of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik and completed in 691 or 692.

facts.made: Ordered by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik; supervised by Raja ibn Haywa and Yazid ibn Sallam with his son Baha, using expert workers from Syria and Egypt who were presumably Christians
facts.form: An octagonal shrine with a dome about 20 metres across on a drum carried by 16 supports, two ambulatories round the rock, four entrances, 36 windows and about 1,200 square metres of mosaic
facts.where: At the centre of the Al-Aqsa mosque compound on the Temple Mount in the Old City of Jerusalem
facts.known: the earliest surviving major work of Islamic architecture; the Foundation Stone beneath its dome; the earliest inscriptions proclaiming Islam and Muhammad; Umayyad mosaics; Ottoman tilework; a gold-plated dome; its place in Muslim, Jewish and Christian belief

t: Abd al-Malik had the shrine built during the Second Fitna, and its inscription date, 72 AH (691/2), is the year most historians take as the completion of the original building.

Muslims, Jews and Christians each attach significance to the rock beneath the dome: Muslims to the Night Journey of Muhammad, Jews to the Temple, and Christians and Jews to Abraham's attempted sacrifice of his son.
Crusaders made it a church, Saladin reconsecrated it, Suleiman the Magnificent covered its walls in tile, and the Jordanian restoration of 1959 to 1964 gave it its gold-plated roof.
dyk: The dedicatory inscription inside the dome originally named Abd al-Malik, but his name was later removed and replaced by that of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun, while the date 72 AH was left unchanged.
ev: The original dome was completed in 72 AH (691/2), the year most historians accept, on the orders of Abd al-Malik
The upper part of the dome collapsed in an earthquake and was rebuilt in 1022 and 1023 under the Fatimid al-Zahir
Crusaders captured Jerusalem and gave the shrine to the Augustinians, who turned it into a church
Saladin recaptured Jerusalem, reconsecrated the shrine and replaced the cross on the dome with a crescent
Ottoman tiles dated to this year appear on the exterior, part of the renovation begun under Suleiman the Magnificent
Parts of the building collapsed in an earthquake on 11 July and the walls were left badly cracked
Jordan began a restoration that lasted until 1964 and replaced the lead on the dome with gold-plated aluminium-bronze
The gold covering of the dome was refurbished with funds from King Hussein of Jordan

sections.origins:
The Dome of the Rock stands at the centre of the Temple Mount, the site of Solomon's Temple and of the Second Jewish Temple, which Herod the Great greatly expanded in the 1st century BCE. The Romans destroyed Herod's Temple in 70 CE, and after the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 CE the emperor Hadrian built a Roman temple to Jupiter Capitolinus there. Under Byzantine rule from the 4th to the 6th centuries Christian pilgrimage to Jerusalem developed, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre was built in the 320s, but the Temple Mount was left undeveloped after a failed project to restore the Jewish Temple under the emperor Julian.

In 638 the Arab armies of the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab conquered Byzantine Jerusalem. Umar was advised by Ka'b al-Ahbar, a rabbi who had converted to Islam, that the site was identical with that of the former Jewish Temples. Among the first Muslims Jerusalem was called Madinat bayt al-Maqdis, the City of the Temple. The shrine was ordered by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik, who reigned from 685 to 705, during the Second Fitna. Its octagonal plan may have been influenced by the Byzantine-era Church of the Seat of Mary, known as Kathisma in Greek, built between 451 and 458 on the road between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
sections.content:
The plan is essentially octagonal. A dome about 20 metres across, set on an elevated circular drum, stands on 16 supports, four piers and twelve columns. An octagonal arcade of 24 piers and columns surrounds this circle, and the two together form an inner ambulatory encircling the holy rock; the outer octagon forms a second ambulatory. Each outer wall measures about 60 metres wide and 36 metres high. There are four entrances, one for each cardinal direction, and the outer wall has 36 windows.

Mosaics cover about 1,200 square metres of the interior, with stylised plants and trees, geometric patterns and jewellery drawn from late antique Byzantine and Sasanian art. The columns and capitals were reused from older buildings. The Umayyad inscriptions on the octagonal arcades are in early Kufic script and mix Qur'anic passages with the Shahada. One frieze quotes verses from the Qur'an on Jesus, son of Mary, including a rejection of the idea that God should take a child. Outside, the Ottoman tilework carries Surah Ya-Sin, with Surah 17, Al-Isra', which tells of the Night Journey, inscribed above it.
sections.making:
The structure was built by order of Abd al-Malik, and it had basically the same shape as it does today. The date of its start is given differently: Sibt ibn al-Jawzi says construction began in 685/6, and al-Suyuti puts its commencement in 688. A dedicatory inscription in Kufic script gives the year 72 AH (691/2), which most historians believe is the year the original Dome was completed; an alternative reading takes it to be the year construction started. Some scholars have suggested that the dome was added to an existing building, either one built by Muawiyah I or a Byzantine building from the time of Heraclius.

The supervisor and engineer were Raja ibn Haywa, Yazid ibn Sallam and Yazid's son Baha. Abd al-Malik was represented in the supervision by his son Sa'id al-Khayr, and he brought expert workers from across his domain, then restricted to Syria and Egypt. Construction cost was reportedly seven times the yearly tax income of Egypt. The plan and mosaics were patterned on nearby Byzantine churches and palaces; K. A. C. Creswell noted that the builders used the measurements of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
sections.reception:
Medieval sources give varying motives for Abd al-Malik. One series of explanations holds that, at war with Byzantium and with the rival caliph Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who controlled Mecca, he wanted a monument of victory that set Islam apart in a city of older Abrahamic faiths. Shelomo Dov Goitein argued that the rotunda was meant to rival the many Christian domes, and others name the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in particular. A second account holds that he wished to divert Muslims from the Ka'aba, where Ibn al-Zubayr condemned the Umayyads at the pilgrimage. Most modern historians dismiss this as anti-Umayyad propaganda, though others concede that it cannot be conclusively dismissed.

Muslims hold that Muhammad's Night Journey began from the rock. The early sources suggest this was not yet fully formulated when the Dome was built, and its inscriptions of 691/2 do not mention it. Ibn Ishaq, in the early 8th century, wrote that Muhammad ascended to heaven from the Rock. Some Islamic scholars say instead that he ascended from the Masjid Al-Aqsa, of which the Dome is a part. Christians and Jews believe the site is where Abraham attempted to sacrifice his son. Jewish tradition holds it to be where God created the world and Adam.
sections.survival:
Earthquakes damaged the building in 808 and 846, and the upper part of the dome fell in 1015; it was rebuilt in 1022 and 1023 under the Fatimid al-Zahir, who also repaired the drum's mosaics in 1027 and 1028. After the Crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 the Augustinians made the shrine a church. The Templars, who regarded it as the Temple of Solomon, called it the Templum Domini and put it on their Grand Masters' seals, and it became the model for round Templar churches across Europe. Saladin recaptured the city on 2 October 1187, had the Crusaders' marble cover removed from the rock, and reconsecrated the shrine.

The Mamluk sultans restored the exterior and re-gilded the dome, which was severely damaged in 1447. Suleiman the Magnificent replaced the old exterior mosaics with tiles, with inscriptions dated 1545 and 1552. A restoration of 1874 and 1875 replaced tiles on the west and southwest walls. The earthquake of 11 July 1927 caused parts to collapse. Between 1959 and 1964 Jordan led a restoration funded by Arab governments and Turkey, replacing tiles with copies made in Italy. The 1993 refurbishment of the golden covering used 80 kilograms of gold funded by King Hussein.
sections.legacy:
UNESCO designated the Dome of the Rock a World Heritage Site, and its golden dome dominates Jerusalem's skyline. According to the art historian Oleg Grabar it remains a unique monument of Islamic culture in almost all respects, a work of art and a cultural and pious document. Its Islamic inscriptions became a model, as afterwards such inscriptions became a common feature in Islamic structures and almost always mention Muhammad. Its architecture inspired later buildings, including the 15th-century octagonal Church of St. Giacomo in Italy, the Rumbach Street Synagogue in Budapest, the mausoleum of Suleiman the Magnificent in Istanbul and the New Synagogue in Berlin.

The compound is a subject of dispute today. The Dome is maintained by the Ministry of Awqaf in Amman. In 1967, during the Six-Day War, an Israeli flag was raised over it and lowered a few hours later on the orders of Moshe Dayan, who gave the Muslim waqf authority to manage the Al-Aqsa. Under the arrangement known as the Status Quo, non-Muslims may visit at set hours but may not pray there; the Chief Rabbinate of Israel maintains a ban on Jews entering any part of the site.

summary: The Dome of the Rock is an octagonal shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, ordered by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik and completed in 691/2. It has been a church, a Muslim shrine again and a monument of the tilework and gold of later rulers, and it holds meaning for Muslims, Jews and Christians.

notes: Start year: the article gives 685/6 (Sibt ibn al-Jawzi) and 688 (al-Suyuti) for the start of building, and AH 72 (691/2) as the completion that most historians accept, or by another reading the start. 691 is used with circa true.

The article gives the inscribed date 72 AH as 691/2 in most places and as 692-693 once; 691/2 is used. It dates the Fatimid mosaic epitaphs to 413 AH (1027/8) in one place and to 413 and 418 AH (1022-23, 1027-28) in another; the rebuild of 1022-23 and drum repair of 1027-28 are used and the epitaph dates left out.

Left out: the 2026 record visitor figure and other visitation numbers; the Temple Institute and evangelical statements about a Third Temple; the banknote depictions; the Raphael and Perugino paintings; Luxenberg's reinterpretation of the inscription (only listed in the article's bibliography).

The article says the Dome is maintained by the Ministry of Awqaf in Amman, and also that the Israeli-appointed arrangement gave the waqf authority to manage the Al-Aqsa; both are given as bare facts. The article's text on access since 1967 is partly judgemental and was reduced to the Status Quo and the Rabbinate's ban.
The article states the Temple Mount has Jews facing it in prayer and says Muhammad's early prayer direction toward Jerusalem; left out for length.
The 1960-21 restoration date of Mamluk decoration in the article is a typo; left out.
